title: Threat Intelligence Program
summary: A Threat Intelligence Program turns scattered reporting about adversaries into decisions the organisation can act on this week. The mechanism is a pipeline: requirements are defined by the people who own risk, collection pulls from internal telemetry and external feeds, processing normalises and de-duplicates it, analysis adds context about who is targeting the sector and with what tools, and dissemination puts the result in front of an audience that can change a control. In real environments the useful outputs are rarely finished reports. They are detection rules built from observed adversary behaviour, watchlists for hunting, blocking decisions at the perimeter, a short list of the techniques most relevant to the estate, and a briefing that helps leadership accept a costly control. Evidence of value is measurable in detection coverage, mean time to detect, and the number of decisions traceable to intelligence, not in the volume of indicators ingested. The common misunderstandings are that a paid feed equals a programme, and that more indicators equal more security. Indicators expire quickly and are frequently reused or shared across unrelated activity, so indicator-only intelligence produces large blocklists with weak returns. A second misunderstanding is that attribution is the goal. Public attribution is often made with moderate confidence, is contested between vendors, and is rarely actionable on its own, so defensible reporting separates observed behaviour from the judgement about who is responsible.

beginner.definition: Threat intelligence is information about who attacks organisations like yours and how they work. A Threat Intelligence Program is the routine that collects that information, checks it, and turns it into action. The action might be a new alert, a block rule, or a training reminder.
beginner.whyItMatters: You cannot defend against everything equally. You need to know what is likely to come your way. Intelligence helps you spend limited time on the attacks that really target your industry. It also helps you explain to managers why a control matters. Without a programme, feeds arrive as noise and nobody changes anything.
howItWorks: Ask the teams what they need to know, such as which attacker groups target your sector.
Collect information from your own logs and from trusted external sources and industry groups.
Clean the data, remove duplicates, and check how reliable each source has been before.
Analyse the behaviour, not just the addresses, and link it to the systems you actually run.
Share short, useful outputs with the teams who can change a rule or a setting.
Measure whether the intelligence changed a decision, and drop sources that never help.
beginner.example: Think of a weather forecast for a farm. The farmer does not need every measurement from every station in the world. They need to know whether frost will arrive tonight. That decides whether the crops are covered. A good forecast service collects data widely, filters it, and delivers one clear warning. A Threat Intelligence Program works like that forecaster. It turns a flood of raw reports into a few decisions made in time.
takeaways: Start with the questions your defenders need answered, then choose sources that help.
Behaviour lasts longer than addresses, so build detections around how attackers operate.
Judge the programme by decisions changed, not by the number of indicators stored.

objectives: Explain how a threat intelligence programme moves from requirements to action.
Distinguish tactical indicators from strategic and operational intelligence.
Describe how to build detections from adversary behaviour rather than addresses alone.
Assess source reliability and handle conflicting or low confidence reporting.
Explain why public attribution should be presented with care and caveats.
